In pursuance of the power conferred on me by Regulation 11 of the Defence of the Realm (Consolidation) Regullitions .1914, I HEREBY MAKE THE FOLLOWING ORDER:—

(1) Subject to the later provisions of this Order, all external lamps, flares and fixed lights of all descriptions, and all aggregations of lights, whether public or private, must be extinguished, except Such nubile lamps as, in the opinion of the Chief Officer of Police, are necessary for safety and any other lights approved by 'him. All lights which are not extinguished must be reduced to the minimum intensity consistent with safety, and shaded or obscured so as to render them invisible from above, and to cut off direct light in al 1 directions above the hori- zontal.

—(2)The intensity of the inside lighting of shops and shop fronts must he reduced or the lights obscured or shaded. so that no more than a dull .Subdued light" is visible outside, and no part of the pavement or roadway or any build- ing, is distinctly illuminated thereby; in par- ticular, all sources of light must be shaded with some opaque material so that all direct light therefrom is cut off from the windows and doors.

_ (3) In hotel, flats, dwelling-houses, and premises of all. descriptions not coining under other provisions of this Order, inside lights must be so shaded Or reduced, or the windows, skylights and glass doors so screened by shutters or dark blinds or curtains, &c., that'no more than a dull subdued light is visible from any direction outside.

(4) In factories, workshops and other such buildings which are illuminated at night, the roof areas and windows must be covered over or obscured, and the lighting intensity reduced to the minimum necessary for the safe and expe- ditious progress of work: • Provided that lighting may be maintained in armament works and other factories engaged in the manufacture of articles 'required for the fulfilment of Government contracts, to suCh extent as may be necessary for the safe and ex- Teditious progress of work. • (5) The intensity of the lighting of railway stations, sidings, goods yards, docks, &c.. must be reduced to the minimum that will Suffice for the safe and expeditious progress of work; the tops and sides of all external lights which can- -not be dispensed with must be shaded or Painted over.

FARMERS AND COMPULSION. - Certified Agricultural Occupations. The Board of Agriculture and Fisheries has issued a notice to farmers setting forth in sum- mary form the main provisions of the Military Service Act, as .it affects them, and explaining the manner in-which claims for exemption will be dealt with by the local and appeal tribunals. The notice points out that under the Act, Government Departments 7are empowered to certify that men engaged in''certain occnpations (known as "certified occupations ") may be exempted on the ground that the work of such men is work of national importance; and the agricultural occupations, which have been so certified by the Board of Agriculture and Fisheries, are as follows:— Agricultural Engine-men and Mechanics.— Agricultural machinery, steam ploughs. and threshing naaehinee, attendant, driver, mechanic. Farm Workers.—Bailiff, foreman, steward, beastman, byreman, cattleman, stock- man, yardman, carter, horseman, ploughman, teamster, wagoner, hind (if foreman or plough- man), servant (if foreman or ploughman) (Scotland), shepherd, thatcher. Farmers and Market Gardeners.—Farmer (in. eluding market gardener and fruit farmer) pro- vided that (a) farming is his sple occupation and his personal labour or superintendence is indispensable for the proper cultivation of his holding; or (b) if he is- partly occupied in another occupation and his personal labour or superintendence is indispensable for the proper cultivation of his holding, and such cultivation is expedient in the national interest. Hop, Fruit and Market Gardens: Foremen in all departments.
i:

Stud Attendants.—Stallion man (a man who looks after and travels a stallion). Stud Groom (Scotland). It will be seen that these "certified occupa- tions" are the same as those hitherto known as " starred " or " reserved " occupations, with some additions and revisions, notably that of "Farmer (including market gardener and -fruit farmer)." The notice also states that while the cases of men who have attested voluntarily under the "Derby Scheme" do not come within the pro- visions of the Act, it is the intention that the two classes of cases, those of men who came under the Act and those of men who have voluntarily attested, shall be dealt with on the same lines, and the constitution of the existing local tribunals will be modified where necessary for this purpose. New instructions will be issued by the Local Government Iloard for the observance pf local tribunals in dealing with these cases, and such instructions will supersede those previously made. div.head: DAIRY CATTLE.
div.p: DAIRY CATTLE.

• Dairy cows cost a lot to keep at this season of the year, and must be reasonably well fed if the milk supply is to be maintained. But consider- able economy can be effected if they are fed with concentrated food in direct proportion to their milk supply, as it is a mistake to imagine that extra heavy feeding will induce an economical increase in the yield of milk, and .if the,quan- tity of milk obtained does not pay for the,heavy cost of the foods, then the feeding is being done at a loss. Cows giving only 2 gallons of milk per head per day should have no more than 41b. of cakes and meals per head per day; those giv- ing up to 4 gallons per head per day will put 61b. to gOod use, while only those giving up to 6 gallons per day will pay for the inclusion of as much as 81b. of concentrated foods in their ration.—" Farm and Home."

div.head: Peas and Broad Beans.
div.p: Peas and Broad Beans.

Land should be got ready for the above as soon as possible.- Trenches about 12 to 14 inches wide are _best for peas and beans, adding old turves at the bottom 'and plenty of well-rotted manure. For light soil, cow manure is best and horse manure for heavy soils. Peas should be sown in rows three inches from seed to seed and about four to five rows in a drill. It is foolish- nesa to scatter peas in drills because some are tvercro*deel.and never get enough nourishment, the result being small pods; only half filled. The first week in March .is early enough for first earlies and every fortnight afterwards. Grand varieties are; Little Marvel and Laxtonian lift.; Gradus, 34ft. The latter is still the finest early marrowfat pea yet raised. Second eirlies are Daisy, 2ft.; Senator, 3ft.; Gladstone, Cen- tenary and Quite,Content, from four to six feet. I think Daisy is the- beet second early, pea, its flavour being very good. Ot late peas, No Plus Ultra, eft., is the best. For small gardens the dwarf varieties shotrld be grown, say up to 2ft. in height. Theae can be staked with rope, net- ting, &c. Soil up when ina. high, and put black cotton around and over to keep the spar- rows from eating the lot.

div.head: Broad Beans.
div.p: Broad Beans.

The culture is like peas. Sow from gin. to 12in. apart in rows diagonally, • and when 3in. high soil up. Two rows will be plenty in a drill, 12 to 14 inches wide. It is a great mistake to sow these too close. When third or fourth lot of flowers are on, pinch all tops off and stop weak basal shoots from growing, these only take nourishment from the main stem. This pinch- ing off is a good preventive from black fly. The best cure for black and green fly, Scc., is XL All insecticide; for use see directions on bottle, ob- tainable from all seedsmen. The best variety of broad beans is Bunyard's Exhibition. This variety gives long pods often 12ia. long, contain- ing beans of good flavour, with six to nine in a pod. Other good varieties are Johnson's Long Pod, Taylor's Broad Windsor and Green Wind- Bor. Sow broad beans at once. These, like peas, are fond of lime.

Tramcar Runs Into Man In A
Fit.
"Never argue with a woman, it's a mistake," was the advice of Mr. S. Brighouse (coroner) to a witness at an inquest held at the Warrington' Police Station on Saturday morning.

The inquiry related to -Thomas -Cunningham (54). tanner, of 283, Wigirick-road, Warrington, who was caught by the cow-catcher of a tpim and died on Thursday. Mrs. Agnes Wade, a sister of Cunningham, admitted that her brother was subject to fits, but said that at the Infirmary he told her the tram had knocked him down.

John Henry Cook: 10, Houghton-street, War- rington, said he was driving the tramcar, and when he was in Winwick-street he noticed a motor cycle coming towards him and sounded his bell as a warning. After the cycle had passed, he noticed an object lying, between the tramlines. It was then about ten yards in front of his car-. He applied the emergency brakes immediately, but felt a bump. Ile went round and there found Cunningham. The night was dark, rain was drizzling, and, owing to the darkened streets, it was impossible to see far ahead.

Mr. Lythgoe, of Longford-stfeet, said he saw Cunningham lying in the road when the car was only a few yards off. The driver pulled uj within five yards. Mrs. Wade began to question this witness, and said that if he saw Cunningham in the road, it was his place to have picked him up. As Lythgoe was about to reply to one of her questions. Mr. Brighouse stopped him, saying, "Take my advice, never argue with a woman; it is a mistake."

Mrs. Wade: I say he was knocked down by the car. ' The Coroner remarked that he did Rot attaen much importance to the statement of the rela- tives, because they were hardly in a logical frame of mind, ,though, he -did not blame them for. uttering their expressions. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death," there being no blame attached to any- one.

SUCCESS II THE PGULTRY YARD.
Rearing Chickens In Dry Grain.
By E. T. BROWN.

One of the inevitable drawbacks to the early rearing of chickens is that there is always a danger of mortality ranging high. Nearly all of this difficulty arises from the ,fact that the birds won't take sufficient exercise. There are many occasions when the weather is nclement —it is raining, or cold easterly winds are blow- ing—when the birds are better under cover all day long, and these are the times during which it is so extremely difficult to keep the youngsters busily occupied. And yet, if they are to develop strong frames and sound constitutions, constant and abundant exercise is imperative.

Where the Dry Method Of Feeding Scores. The old method of feeding young chickens— supplying them with soft food in troughs rather encourages- laziness than otherwise, since the birds speedily satisfy their appetites; and merely mope in the corners of the brooder. This difficulty is entirely surmounted when the dry method is adopted, for the chickens are kept busily occupied throughout the entire day. If they do not work, and work continuously, they have to go hungry, and there can be no greater inducement to exercise than this. Without exercise chickens frequently contract chills, bowel trouble is extremely common, and during a long spell of bad weather, or in a ideation where the conditions are somewhat unfavour- able, mortality range,' high. Advantages and Drawbacks. . The great advantage of this system lies in the increased vitality and the greater health of the chickens. But there are other advantages. Under the moist method of feeding one is con- stantly preparing food for the birds, from early morning till late at night, for during the first week or two of their lives th-y require feeding every two or three hours from about 6.30 a.m. until about 9 p.m.; under the dry method sufficient food is scattered once a day to last the birds for the twenty-four hours. It is pos- sible for a man to attend to Jour or fiye times as many chickens as he could When "feeding upon soft foods. Another advantage, is that the cost of feeding is reduced, and every penny that can be saved in this respect represents increased. profits. There are two disadvantages of this method of feeding, but they are of cOmpara- tively small importance. Chickens do not grow quite so rapidly, at"; Whbn they are fed upon soft foods, but this is only natural when it is re- membered that they are working all day long. The increased health .and vigour far more than outweighs this drawback. Another drawback is that the system lends itself so readily to waste. At any time, this should be avoided; it is little short of criminal at the present moment to waste a single grain. I have often examined the chaff in a brooder, and have found that there Was a layer half an inch or an inch thick, of grain lying below the chaff;

How the System is Worked. The floor of the brooder or coop—for the system is -suitable for both artificially and naturally reared chickens—is covered with chaff two or three inches deep, and the food is scat- tered thereamong, for which the chickens bar-) to scratch. There are some very good preparl- tions of dry chick.feed ow the market, but th,).-e who prefer to do so can mix their own, and t.'43 following is one which I have used extensively for some years past, and which has given goo I results: Three parts wheat; two parts each dari, pinhead oatmeal, canary :seed and millet; and one part each maize, buckwheat, rice, grit and meat. Counting one part as 71b., the abo re works out to icwt. The wheat, buckwheat ao 1 maize require to be cracked, since whole th..*, cannot be properly digested. This diet shout! continue till the birds are a month old,- for many experiments in this country ;have proved that at the end of a month two meals of soft food should be supplied daily. After Four Weeks.

As soon as the chickens are a month old, two meals a day of soft food should be provided, one first thing in the morning, and another about 3 p.m. One of the many specially prepared chicken foods, ground oats, barley. meal and middlings, are all suitable, either mixed or fed separately. They should be moistened with water or sweet skim 'milk into n crumbly moist condition. A cheaper mixture of grains should be employed, and the following I can recommend: Three parts each of cracked wheat, cracked maize and dart; two parts each of buckwheat and meat; one part each of millet, linseed and grit. A liberal. supply of green food is necessary from the very first; without it the blood becomes heated, and the internal organs refuse to perform their work in a satisfactory manner. Drinking water, too, must be generously provided, and it should be renewed two or three times a day.

'Tis passing strange that while on one page of last week's issue we read of Alderman John Evans blushing at the Town Council meeting and of a soldier at the Brabazon Society's sale "blushing like an American Baldwin apple," on another was explained a process whereby for a consideration the ladies may be provided with a blush that won't come off! 0 tempora, 0 mores! Rival Committees And Power
Of Appointment.
MR. KINGDON VINDiCATED

Mr. Holman Kingdon, who, a few months ago, resigned the chairmanship of the Medical In- spection Sub-committee of the Education Com- mittee because of the action of the Health Committee (supported by the Town Coun- cil) in claiming the right to appoint certain health officials engaged in education work and paid for by the Education Committee, has ex- plained his attitude to the Warrington Chamber of Commerce, which body he represents on the Education Committee, and gave the reasons for his resignation. Mr. Kingdon's action was approved by voice and vote of the Chamber in annual meeting assembled on Monday.

div.head: PROLONGED CONTROVERSY.
div.p: A PROLONGED CONTROVERSY.

Mr. Kingdon said he was chairman of the Medical Inspection Sub-committee from Novem- ber, 21st, 1910, to June 7th, 1915, when he. resigned. In January, 1908, the Education Com- mittee approved a scheme for the medical in- speetion of school children and for attending to ' their health and physical condition. In 1911 a schoild: treatment clinic was inaugurated, and in 1912 a dental clinic was started. Under the scheme of 1908, the Medical Officer. of H'ealth became chief n:Wical officer of the Education Committee, and provision was made for the appointment of an assistant school medical officer and a school nurse to work under his supervision. The Town Council refused to sanction that scheme; but approved a report of the Health Committee, who provided • for the appointment of an assistant medical officer of health, the Medical Inspection Sub-committee to be responsible for dealing with cases after inspection, and to make their own arrangements as to remedial measures. The Education Com- mittee reluctantly agreed, and requested the Health Committee of the Council to proceed with the appointment. The Health Committee made the appointment, • and subse- quently appointed a • school nurse. These officials devoted a considerable amount of their time .to the treatment of minor ailments at the school clinic. When the dental clinic was established the Education Committee appointed a part-time delntist and a ,lady at- tendant, the Council taking no exception to this action; but ih 1911, when the growth of the work necessitated the appointment of a fully-qualified nurse, • the Education Committee minute, authorising the appointment was withdrawn owing to the opposition of the Council, on the claim of the Health Committee to make such appointments. A joint committee to make the appointments was suggested; ..but the Health Committee reported that a joint committee was "not desirable," and proceeded to appoint a nurse. In the interests of the children he and his committee made the best of these things. (Hear, hear.) After many efforts oil the part of the Education Committee to find a way out, 'the Health Committee appointed in October, 1914, a full-time dentist, without saying anything about it.

"And when," continued Mr. Kingdon, "the dentist arrived in the town to take up his work —work for which we were responsible by Statute to the town—you will hardly believe me, gentlemen, when! tell you that we did not even know his name or the date when he was sup- posed to enter on his duties. (Laughter.) An Impossible Situation.

• " The position therefore was that we were asked to be responsible is a committee for the results of work done by, officials in whose appointment we had no voice or influence, a course of action which has not commended itself to any other town or borough in the United Kingdom, and which is neither calculated to produce efficiency nor to be in the best interests of the children themselves. This state of affairs was so-impossible that I felt I haid no option but to resign, and my action was followed alm9st immediately by the resignation of four other members of the committee.

"I wish to say here that until we apply the same principles in our municipal life as would commend themselves to running our own busi- ness we shall not obtain those.results which the age we live in Mid the necessities of the chil- dren themselves require. "Throughout the whole period I have had the cordial support of my own committee, including, I am glad to.say, some members of the Health Committee, and the whole of the facts as briefly outlined above have been laid before the -,Board of Education by the Chairman of the Warring- ton Education Committee?'

There was, in his opinion, no doubt that the Education Committee has been invested by Parliament with certain Statutory rights and duties, and the Statutory provisions ought to be observed. He did not believe that under Section 13 (1) (b) of the Education (Administrative Pro- visions) Act, 1907, the Health Committee had any Statutory status for the purpose of making appointments.to the school medical service or otherwise, and unless the Town Council were prepared to allow this medical work in connec- tion with the school children, which had been built up slowly but surely, with considerable trouble and no little expense, to be run on busi- ness lines, the responsibility must rest with others than himself. (Hear, hear.) ACTION RATIFIED.

I. In conclusion, Mr. Kingdon remarked that he had felt very strongly that there was no good going on any longer. (Hear, hear.) The Chairman (Mr. J. J. Whitley) : It seems ' to have been an impossible situation, and Mr. Kingdon did the only thing he could do. Mr. C. E. Parker alsoi thought Mr. Kingdon was quite justified n resigning. He (Mr. Parker) being on the same committee, had taken a similar course. The position was an altogether impossible one. They were invested with certain responsibilities and were denied the rights which ought to have accompanied and• made effective those responsibilities. Mi. Parker, therefore, moved the adoption of Mr. Kingdon's report, and •
Mr. J. Rymer Young seconded. That a com- mittee which had to provide practically all .the money and have no voice in the spending of it, he said, was a grotesque and Gilbertian situa- tion.

The report having been adopted, Mr. F. A. Frost proposed a resolution, carried unani- mously, approving Mr. Kingdon's action in resigning the chairmanship of the Medical In- spection Sub-committee, and.. expressing,.. the hoPe that• the Town Council 'would see the desirability of giving the control of the work to the committee which was legally responsible for it, if only from a business point of view,

A review of our position industrially and a plea for national, municipal and personal economy were made by the Vice-president (Mr. J. J. Whitley) at the annual meeting of the Warrington Chamber of Commerce, in Market Gate Chambers, on Monday. First, however, he congratulated the Chamber on the acqursition of their new premises. They were very suitable for their purpose, and he hoped that now the offices were in a much more prominent position, more of their fellow traders would be induced to join and have the benefit of excellent facilities. The advantages of hav- ing a really strong Chamber of Commerce were not quite realised in Warrington at present. It was highly important that we should be on the look-out for openings of business which might become possible after the war. Chambers of Commerce would be of great use for that pur- pose. (Hear, hear.) Trade Disorganised.

At present, as at this time last year, trade was constantly in a state of disorganisation, which, although distracting, however, had not caused any very serious difficulties to arise. The most disquieting thing was the enormous in- crease •in the cost of the necessaries of life, which had a constant tendency to rise through the increased cost of freights. Whether that could be avoided was rather hard to say—one did not like to criticise the man at the wheel. (Hear, hear.) Another serious matter was the shortage of labour. This was unavoidable, as we must have every available man for the Army and Navy, bit the difficulty would, doubtless, be minimised to a certain extent by new methods of working. And here, he thought, Chambers of Commeree would be of very great assistance.

In regard to munitions, there was no doubt that the Chamber had been. of very great ser- vice, and, though, as a town, we had had, very little credit for what had been done, we had every reason to be proud of our oUtpat. Preparing For Financial Strain.

In view of the enormous preponderance of imports. for whiCh we were not able to pay with gold at present, it behoved us to confine our purchases to what was mode in England. "There is no doubt that as a nation we are prone to extravagance and luxury," he con- tinued, "and we may well take a lesson from our ally, France. (Hear, hear.) The lesson will be difficult now, but, when we have learned it, it will be to our profit as a nation and as in- dividuals. There is'• not the slightest dopt as to our financial stability, but it is our duty both to practise and preach economy. FRIENDS AND WAR.
Opposition To Compulsory
Service Reaffirmed.

At the recent yearly meeting of the Society of Frienils specially called to consider the situa- tion caused by the Military Service Act, it was decided to "re-affirm our entire opposition to "nlPillsory military service and Our desire for the repeal of the Act." The minute recording this affirmation says : th" War, in our view, involves a surrender of e Christian ideal and a denial of human brotherhood; it is an evil for the destruction of twhhich the world is longing; but freedom from e scourge of war will only be brought about through the faithfulness of individuals to their inmost convictions under the guidance of the Spirit of Christ. Our position is based upon. our interpretation of the teaching of Jesus Christ. We regard the central conception of the Act as imperilling the liberty of the individual con- science—which is the main hope of human pro- gress—and entrenching more deeply that mili- tarism from which we all desire the world to be freed.

"It follows that our opposition is not re- moved by the provisions with regard to con- scierice; ww,elcome as these .are. We have in mind not only conscientious 'objectors, but alsO a large 'nipper hitherto held back from mili- tary peiNiee from no unworthy motive, 'but' kry a restriining influence to which they would find it impossible to give expression. The effeot of coniAlsion' is ruthlessly and indiscriminately to sweep Eill4theBe into the Army. We consider that young men may do import- ant service by going before the Tribunals, Claiming exemption, and making clear their reasons for doing so. At the same time we can- not admit that a human tribunal is an ade- quate judge of any Man's conscience. The final appeal can only be to the source from Which the conscientious convictions themselves Spring. u Our lives should prove • that compulsion is both unnecessary and impolitic. They should In.anifest a sense of duty not less strong than that which has driven many whom we respect, and some even of our own members, into the fighting forces. div.head: CHURCHES AND ZEPPS.
div.p: CHURCHES AND ZEPPS.
The Ruri-Decanal Conference Suggests Insurance.
DARKEN THE WINDOWS.

Concern for their churches during Zeppelin raids was manifested at the Frodsham Ruri- decanal Conference, held in the Church House, Warrington, on Thesday afternoon, and various suggestions for their protection were made. The Rural Dean (the Rev. and Hon. C. F. Cross) said that recently they had been much exer- cised in their minds as to the means they should take, and one method was to have a special insurance. If they could see their way financially, he would advise them to take a policy out immediately. Another idea was to alter the hours of services, those of the evening being hem in the afternoon, so that the glare from the windows would not be a landmark for the Zeppelins. Another way was to darken the windows, and he recommended as a practi- cal and inexpensive mode the placing of brown paper over the windows. There was abso- lutely no need to buy heavy drapery or any- thing expensive.
Asked by a layman how it was possible to insure a beautiful church.

The Rural Dean replied: The churches are irreparable, of course. They are impossible to replace. Under this miserable type of warfare bombs fall hither and thither, and they may hit a sacred building any time. It is best to get them insured. Of course, policies. will cost money, but I think tele people will rally round and help to End it.

div.head: NEW CHURCH AND LIFE AFTER DEATH.
div.p: THE NEW CHURCH AND LIFE AFTER DEATH.
At the Masonic Hall, Bold-street, on Tuesday evening, the Rev. J. Ashby, of Southport, de- livered the first ,of a series of annual New Church lectures, his subject being "Man In Two Worlds."

The attentions of the people were especially drawn to the question at the present time, he said, owing to the large number of people who were passing into the other world consequent upon the clash of arms of so many nations. What became of all those people? The Church had told us that there was heaven and hell, but for information as to the life after death, the Scriptures should be thoroughly examined. We should not just pile up facts but draw prin- ciples from them. A two-fold nature—spiritual and natural—was Possessed by man. The interior was spiritual and the outward natural. Man's body was the existing place of the soul. Men were created in this world for the purpose of having a spiritual body, and unless they had a spiritual body now, they would not have one when they died. The whole of the natural world was God's world, and Was created to prepare us for heaven. It had been said bill Professor Drummond that "this world, if we understood it well, was a perfect model of the other," and all this was a manifestation of the Divine love in the other world. Man-did not really die, for death was only a change. Disaster, suffering and sorrow were sent to show us that our only safety_was in what God had taught us Himself. The cause of death was that the interior man could not be further developed.

Tracing the hisiory of Prussia during- the past few centuries, Mr. Keeling noted that in 1640 Prussia was' of as little importance to Europe as Montenegro is to-day. div.p: A One-Man Show.

By the time of his death Frederick had man- aged to raise an army of thirty thousand highly-trained men. He was succeeded by his son Frederick the First, and again it was a "one-man show." This king was 'followed by his son, known as "Fat William," who quar- relled with his father, a tradition that has been followed down to the present time. A Crown Prince may agree with his grandfather, but not with his father. The next king was Frederick the Great. He was the greatest captain of his age, and was not troubled about scruples. He annexed Silesia and invaded Saxony. His strategy consisted of rapid and unexpected movements, and he certainly was a great man in his way. He took all he could get, and did not care a penny-piece as to whether his methods were honourable or not. His doctrine was "mankind will move if you drive them on, and they will stop as soon as you cease driv- ing them."

Referring to the Napoleonic wars, Mr. Reel- ing said Prussia was crushed as much as any nation could be; its overthrow was complete. Its army was reduced, and its Ministers were chosen by Napoleon. Then ensued the War of Liberation, not carried out so much by the Government, but by the people. " After these wars, the old method of keeping down the people was persisted in, and the political as- pirations of the people were crushed.
Bismarck Called in.

In 1862 there was a majority of' Progressives' in the Howie of Representatives. They re- jected.a Finance' Bill,:. Which. had for it& object the enlargement and equipment of the, Prussian Army: In the deadlock- Bismarck- was called in. --He so. played.off one 'party against another that the old kingly power was restored; The franchise was 'so arranged that, no'matter What .the number of voters, it Was never pos- sible for the working classes to have a majority in the House of Representatives. It was not now; it was not before the war. The number of votes a man had was' proportionate to his income.

After the quarrel with Denmark, Austria and Prance, came the years of manufacture.. The whole thing was an absolutely artificial struc- ture worked from the top. It was not that the nation had suddenly developed commercial power. They were ordered to do it, and the Government provided a greater part of the money. He.could not prove it, but he had been told over and over again, that if one wanted to start a big manufacturing industry in Prussia, the Government would guarantee any leans'that one needed, and the banks would be ordered to find the money _on. the pledge of the Govern- ment. The whole thing was controlled from the top, as though the nation was a big factory controlled by one brain. He hoped one result of the war would be that Germany no longer would be a one-man show. The ._people had ,been trained so 'that political power was almost an impossibility for them, and nOw the intellect and genius of Germany were controlled by the materialistic and tyran- nical Prussia.

The Trades Council have, as was generally expected, decided to defy the' widely- expressed opinion of trade unionists in War- rington that they have acted , beyond their powers in passing the. resolution a few weeks ago condemning the Military Service Bill and pledging themselves to oppose it to the utter- meat. Before we proceed to discuss the merits and demerits of the question once again we shou' ld like to clear the ground a little. Mr. Charles Dukes,. who happens to be the secretaiy of the Trades and Labour Council, and was their main champion at the -meeting held on Tuesday night, accused "The 'Ex- aminer" of having introduced personal animus into the controversy. That state- ment is as untrue as, we believe; his policy is a mistaken One. We do not know Mr. Dukes except as the secretary of the Trades Council, and it is with policy and not persons that we have endeavoured to deal. He says we asked "Who is the Trades Council?" and in reply he asks "Who' is 'The', Examiner '?" His statement here is again untrue. We asked "For whom do the Trades Council speak?" That is the question we still ask, a question which .we fancy the trade unionists Of .War-. rington will now answer in no uncertain manner.

For trade unionists will now ,be able to see exactly where they are. Some of them, as witness the Wiredrawers and the Operative Bakers, have gone to the extreme length of leeeding rather* than be accounted jointly re- sponsible .for a gigantic libel upon them and their fellows, which would have the world believe • that. Warrington, working men are antagonistic to the policy of the -Government and the military authorities in their final. effort- to save our land from disaster, perhaps ruin. Others, like the Postmen and the Co- operative employes, have asked the Trades Council to take the opinion of the trade unions on the question, and have held their , hand in the meantime. Others have threat- ened to secede; and again' others, still out- side the Trades Council, have declined; in view of what-has happened, tojoin the Council "as at, present-constituted." But they are all wrong. 'What -they say is "irrelevant.'? They are "very poorly informed indeed:'? They are thinking by proxy, and "The Ex- aminer" is leading them astray: The facts are "all against -the Postmen." Indeed, according to Mr. Charles Dukes, the whole regiment is' out of step, ercePt.himself and the LieW • mem who, :along -with him; have dared to put an awful aspersion upon the workers of the town, and now dare to, adhere to the position they have taken up. How illogical that position is may be imagined from one other loose utterance which -Mr. Dukes digni- fied by the name of argument. He complained that the Labour party had joined in the re- oruiting movement without consulting him and others; locally, he claims that thirty-six inen—or a majority of tliirtf-six men_Lhal the right to pledge the trade 'unionists of War- ringtim to hostility to an Act that the majority believe to be in the best interests of the country. We invite our readers' special attention to Mr., Dukes' comparison of condi- tions in this country with Prussian condi- tions. It is a fair example to show the state of mind that leads to -such ends. as the offend- ing-resolution which was • forced upon us in ord.er to round up' a series of many acts of atodied disloyalty. Mr.- Dukes- etidently-glorieS in the fact that; he kept his hat on 'before a erovid" of' 145-all-Ai.' singing the National Anthem in front of the Town Hall and in the presence of the 'Mayor, the local representative of. the dignity .of..

the Crown. •He does not know why we re- called that incident, and asks, " After all, what does it matter?" We will tell him. We recalled it to show that he and his friends did not represent the people for whom they are now pilesuming to speak. It matters because the King is the embodiment of the State we love and hope to see survive—and if Mr. Dukes and his friends do not see that it matters, they are still further off than ever from representing us.. There was something else that did not matter. It did not matter, he said, that he was at the bottom of the poll because he has " no desire to get on the Coun- cil of. your rotten borough." Then why did he put the town to the turmoil of an election at a time when all classes were enjoined to maintain internal calm and peace? The only answer is that, agitator-like,, he desired to have a fight at any cost. . But we return to our first question. For whom do these twenty-two men speak when they decide to maintain this obnoxious reso- lution on the books of the Trades Council? We learn that the Engineers meet on Monday and there can be little doubt, but that they will decide to rid themselves of their share of the responsibility. The Town Council this week ignored the Trades , Council when they had in hand the appointment of. a new Tri- bunal to administer the new Act, but the representatives of the t ,radeuriions were called together, and from their nominations Labour representation was gained, which, on a pre- vious occasion, was missed through the "neutral" behaviour a. Labour's vaunted "champions" of. the Trades, Council. Clearly the Trades Council "as at present consti- tuted" are beyond hope; what has happened this week will finally convince the trade uni ms of the absolute necessity of creating a •.entral organisation that would at , once command their confidence and uphold the dignity of genuine Labour.

div.head: DEATH OF MR. VIM. CARSON.
div.p: DEATH OF MR. VIM. CARSON.
Whitecross Chairman Succumbs To Heart Failure.

Mr. William Carson, M.1.C.E., chairman of the Whitecross Co., Limited, wire manufac- turers, Warrington, died of heart failure in his eightieth Year, last Saturday morning, at his residence, Bryn Estyn, Hough Green Chester. Mr. Carson came to Warrington 38 years ago as managing director at Whitecross, in suc- cession to the late Mr. Robert Wallace Murray. a position which he held with success and distinction .till the latter end of last year, when he resigned, his active connection with the firm being assured by his appointment as Chair- man of the Board of Directors. Although he did not take a very prominent part in public affairs, the commanding position he occupied in the concerns of one of our greatest industrial undertakings made him a man of mark, and his sudden withdrawal will cause much regret among a large circle of business men. He was accounted a man of stern nature, but those who knew him best say that he had his more sympa- thetic side, and that his reserve was counter- acted by other qualities, lie was a vice-presi- dent and life governor of the Warrington In- firmary, and was always ready to do a kindly act privately and unostentatiously.
As -President of the Whitecross Works Social and Recreation Club, the late Mr. Carson took great interest in the welfare of the employes, and as a mark of appreciation the members of

the club presented him with his portrait in 1912. The Men's Club and Boy Scouts were other institutions in connection with the works in which he was deeply interested. Mr. Carson was an- amatOtir musician of much ability, and in his early days played the organ and composed many pieces of church music, chiefly hymns and chants. ,

In 1864, Mr. Carson, who was a. brother of the late Rev. James Carson, M.A., rector of War- grave,' married Harriet Elizabeth, second daughter of Staff-Surgeon Simeon Henry Hardy, o Queenstown, and he leaves a Widow, two sons and six daughters. . He was a Conservative.

"Holy Trinity Parish Magazine," referring to the death of Mr. Wm. Gilt says:—" He is a- great loss to the Church in many ways—net least by his example. Mr. Shimmin said there were one or two points he wanted to make clear to Mr: Dukes. He (the speaker) did not understand the re- fusal of a plebiscite, fOr• the trade unionists paid the piper. Mr.. • The news has this week been received by Mrs. Sankey, of 39, Sharp-street, Warrington, that her brother, Rifleman Thomas Molloy, of the Post Office Rifles, Bth City London Division, has been killed in action.
Rifleman Molloy, familiarly known to his associates as "Mull," was an old Volunteer, and enlisted for service in July of last year,
being • eventually drafted. to France in the first Week of -November following. Prior to the war he was employed at the Warrington Post Office, where he had served fora quarter of a century. .

The news of his 'death was first communi- cated to/his sister by two of the deceased's com- rades, Rifleman P. J. Webb and Rifleman A. Norry, who are in the same regiment. They stated: "He was going along the trenches with his Corporal, When shell came over, killing them instantly. We don't think poor Tom suf- fered any pain. Rifleman Molloy, who was 39 years of age, attended St. Alban's School as xt. :youth and worshipped at the St.- Benedict's Church, where he was highly .esteeined and admired. div.head: LABOUR REPRESENTATION.
div.p: LABOUR REPRESENTATION.
Trades Council Ignored; Unions Consulted. '

At the invitation of the Mayor, a meeting of the chairmen and secretaries of the local Tr Unions was held in the Town Hall on Thursd.ty evening, to nominate representatives of labour to sit on the Warrington Tribunal, to be appointal under the Military Service Act, 1916. The Mayor presided, and the Deputy Town Clerk (Mr. A. T. Hallaway) acted as secretary. . _

At the outset the Mayer- said he had called them together in what he considered to be the spirit of the Military Service Act. It was necessary on all Tribunals, indeed it was desir- able, that labour should be represented. In the ordinary way the Council had full power to nominate any one whom they considered the representatives of labour, but the Towti Council did not know everything about labour, and the meeting had been called to ask for names, with a 'view of submitting them to the Council, of gentlemen who would probably look after the interests of labour and give a fair and judicial hearing and decision on th,e various appeals that would come before the Tribunal. He did not desire any speeches or arguments, but he wanted names that he could submit to the Council. The Mayor was immediately bombarded with a series of questions. One delegate asked, that if the meeting nominated three gentlemen, would. the Council accept them. The reply was that it was the business of the Council to select the members of the Tribunal, mar: zne Mayor could not pledge them to do anything. Another questioner wanted to know if the gentlemen nominated should be above military age or be exempted.
The Mayor replied that men who were not *willing to serve would hardly be eligible to sit on ho Tribunal, but, of course, that would be a matter for the Council.
In nominating a wiredrawers' representative, another dejegate was about to make a speech. He said "The wiredrawers have proved them- selves loyal 11
The Mayor: I don't. want anything pf that sort.
Advocating the claims of another gentleman, a .delegate referred to his' position in the Trades and Labour Council.
The Mayor replied he was ignoring tho Trades and Labour Council, otherwise he would not have called the meeting. Nine nominations were received.

div.head: CORPORAL S. LINLEV.
div.p: CORPORAL S. LINLEV.
Ex-Local Preacher Home On A Well-Earned Furlough.

Corporal Sid. Linley visited hi g home at Pepper-street, Lymm, on Tuesday, from Win- chester, after returning from the Front. It will be remembered that the gallant Corporal was wounded in the back in April last, and returned again to the Front in 'September. only to have the misfortune to be taken ill with nephritis, shortly after arrival. - Corporal Linley is a married man with two children, and in' civil life is an insurance agent: He is widely known as a Nonconformist worker and local preacher, being connected with the Lymm Wesleyan Church. Corporal Linley, who was one of the audience at the Y.M.C.A. auction sale on Thursday even- ing, says words cannot adequately express the good work both spiritually and materially done by the Y.M.C.A. at the Front. The concert parties are of the best, and nothing can repay the work done. Harmless Disturbers.

Relating his experience, he mentioned a time When he was on guard, and the sentry, hearing a rushing sound, at once gave the challenge, but received no response; he again challenged, and again he received no response. On the guard being turned out they. found to their disgust, nothing but three calves which had strayed from their grazing place! The gallant Corporal returns, to his depot at Chester on the 19th. and "eipects ,to ,be drafted to the Front again shortly.

The Daresbury Brewster Sessions were held at Stockton Heath on Tuesday, but apart from the presentation of Supt. Owen's report, the busi- ,ness was purely-formal. The magistrates preSent were Messrs. F. .A. Frdst, Henry Roberts, J. Hepherd, W. Fletcher, J. Baxter. J. A. Ransome and W. Antwis.

Seventeen persons had been proceeded against for drunkenness, all being convicted, as com- pared with twenty-five proceeded against and twenty-four convicted during the preceding year. Of the-seventeen persons convicted for drunken- ness during the year ended December 31st; 1915, sixteen were males. That showed a decrease of eight males when compared with the previous year. Frost: It is very satisfactory to see that crime has gone down so much, and I hope it will continue to go down in the future.

ORFORD MEN.
Varying Experiences In All Areas Of The War.
(Extracts from the Orford, Parish Magazine.)

"The Germans sent gas oi-er hero the other day. But we are up to all their tricks now, and they got the biggest surprise in their lives. We chaps from Orford are getting quite strong; we shall soon have an army of our own. Good luck to them all." Met "Orford Boys."

"It is quite a pleasure to hear from the dear old folks of Orford. I met two of the Orford boys on Saturday—Will Swinton and Jack Povey—and I must say they looked well. I suppose I shall be going up to the front again soon. Hoping and trusting in God to help me on my way." Decent Christmas Spread.

"We spent quite a unique time out here this Christmas. For •a start we had our Christmas dinner on the Thursday, two days beforehand, owing to us receiving sudden orders to move. But. wq had it pretty decent spread considering ,the circumstances. We were on the move at two'n'chick" in the morning of Chri4tinas Eve, and after marching about eight miles in pour- ing rain, we entrenched, and then it became fine. We were riding in the train for between fifty and sixty hours and we spent our Christ- mas Day-in a.horse van." "

div.head: Stuck In The Mud.
div.p: Stuck In The Mud.

"Coming back was the job. All the way we were in range of the enemy. I had started to come hack .and had gone about 200 yards when I Sank up to the waist in mud. I couldn't move, and I Couldn't shout to the others who were in front, as I might have been heard, and then I should have got it hot. There I stuck until goodness knows how long, and was very glad to biter the Other two coming back for me. They had missed me On entering the trench and had come back to look for me."

div.head: How Was It Allowed To Happen?
div.p: How Was It Allowed To Happen?

• "Well, my Christmas was spent as the New Year will be—close up behind the trenches, helping to make the way a little safer for our comrades who have to hold them. As the day brake an Christmas morn, my thoughts went back to little Orford, and I thought of the hoisting of the flag, and the singing of Christ- mas anthems On the Tower. I looked at the remains of the church.here—two walls and half of the tower, `with the vaults half opened, and the graves and stones upturned—and tried to solve the problem of how it all was allowed to happen." -
'From Desert To Snow.

"I am not in Egypt now, but in the Balkans. We had a great change here after being en- camped on a scorching, hot desert for four weeks, and then to be transferred here, with snow about eight inches deep. It nearly put us out first stroke.. We are just settling down now, though, and hope to be soon acclimatised. I have dropped across one friend from War- rington out here in the A.0.C., in the person of Mr. Roberts, from Dallam-lane. I met him in Salonika, and he was delighted to have• a chat with me."

div.head: " Don't Believe It."
div.p: " Don't Believe It."

"I have often heard that the R.A.M.C. never go near the trenches, but don't believe it, for they go farther than the trenches and dress wounds, then'carry the wounded down about five miles over hilly country, full of snipers. We have lost a lot of men, poor chaps, but they have done their bit, and done it well—God bless them—and we will take their place."

div.head: Bit of Excitement.

"We had a bit of excitement this morning. Our airmen brought a German `Albatros 'down. - It lauded in the 'field, where we are bivouacked. div.head: VIGILANT POLICE.
div.p: VIGILANT POLICE.
Visits To Licensed Premises Has Satisfactory Results.

." Generally satisfactory" was the Mayor's comment at the Brewster Sessions, yesterday, regarding the use of intoxicants last year in the borough. He pointed out that whereas in 1915 the num- ber of people who were convicted for drunken- ness was 586, the total in 1914 was 615. In 1913 it was 544. When we came to analyse the
figures even the increase of eases over 1913

turned out satisfactorily to Warrington, for of the 586 cages only 224 were residents, the re- maining 362 being .strangers who came here to get drunk. This was an increase of 91 in strangers, as compared with last year, and a decrease of 120 in residents. By some people it might be attributed to the war, but in 1913 209 strangers were dealt with, whereas last year we had 362. In 1913 we had 345 residents, and in 1915 224. 'Therefore, there was an in.2rease of strangers and a decrease of Warringtonians. So if the war affected Warrington it only affected strangers.. 'Police Visits To Licensed Premises.

div.head: HEATHSIDE TOO GOOD FOR BOLTON.
div.p: HEATHSIDE TOO GOOD FOR BOLTON.

Heathside and Bolton met at Wilderspool be- fore a good crowd. The ground was rather on the soft side, but the weather conditions were ideal. Heathside won the toss and set Bolton to face a strong sun. From the opening ,kick - the %all' was returned to midfield. A passing movement resulted in the Heathside right-wing getting away, but when becoming dangerous was neatly checked by Jones, the Bolton full-back, who, with a good ran, averted all danger. Heathside came again, and from a melee on the line the ball was carried over. Rutter completed the try. Harter kicked the goal, thus Heathside were five points to the good after ten minutes' play. This roused. Bolton, who, from the restart, bore down upon their opponents' line. Heathside, however, defended gamely, and, from a scrim- mage, 'they commenced a passing movement, which again took them into Bolton territory. By two free-kicks awarded them, Bolton came away, and Jones, with a fine individual effort in which he beat several players, took play to the quarter-line. Here he was obstructed, and the referee promptly awarded the Boltonites a free- kick. This was taken by Hart, who opened Bolton's account.

div.head: Opening Lost.
div.p: Opening Lost.

Immediately after the restart Heathside were awarded free-kick for obstruction. A cross- kick was put in, and,-,the Heathside left-wing had a fin opportunity of scoring. Instead of running straight,•however, he• elected _to , double,- in, with ' the result that he was 'promptly tackled. From a scrimmage Heath- side worked their way to the line, where they obtained possession of the ball. One of their players immediately essayed to dash over, and a try seemed imminent. Jones, however, flung himself at his opponent and, tackling excellently, brought him down. Good fer Ward - play worked the ball away, and, when putting in a good run, the Bolton right-wing was badly obstructed. Harter was the offender. and he was immediately ordered from the field. Even play followed, and Jones made another fine run. He was playing a great game, and, time after time, turned defence into attack by means of his tricky runs. A Heath- side player was cautioned for foul play in the "pack," following which, after a hot attack. Forster scored for Heathside. The goal-kick failed, and half-time found them leading by eight points to' two. , '
Bolton Desperate In Second Half.

Heathside commenced the second half, and Jones, making another effort for Bolton, was nearly over. A scrimmage,was formed on the line, from which the ,ball went dead. Bolton were now playing desperately, and they forced two dead balls in as many minutes. Once they should have scored easily, but, when a few yards from the line,. a player 'elected to kick instead of dashing through. Thus, this chance—one of the finest of the match—was lost. Just before time Heathside scored again through McAvoy, Lingard goaling. Thus the game ended a-win for Heathside by two goals, three tries, 13 points, to Belton's one goal, two points.

div.head: ASSOCIATION.
div.p: ASSOCIATION.
THE TOWN SECURE THEIR FIRST VICTORY.
Score Well Against Walkden.

Many good games have been witnessed this season in the Lancashire Combination, but for keenness, exhilaration and excellence that be- tween the Town and Walkden C.-ntral on Sat- urday was one of the best. We came away wtth five goals, leaving them with two. To-day we ale to meet.tlieng at Hood-lane. If the game proves as interesting as last week there wlll be no disappointment, although criticism may be forthcoming. The best team a commit!ee ever made needs it.

The enjoyment of the spectators at Walkden was evidenced by the "voices" of the crowd, which numbered over 2,000. Of course, both clubs had to win their first match, bo there were reasons why both should strain every effort to bring off the spoils. .The home teim played a really keen game; in fact, rather too keen at times.

Although they commenced two men short for the first fifteen minutes, Walkden's defence was. magnificent, but as an attacking fore() they were never equal to the Town, who, without the least exaggeration, were invincible on the day's play, and had more than three-parts of the game. It was to their defence, in particu- lar, that Walkden could attribute the fact that they were not more heavily defeated.

Not one team in the Combination could have beaten the Town on this play, and even the display of the home team surprised their directors. Kite, the Town custodian, was simply brilliant and unflinching.. The backs— Leah and Cookson—were equally relentless and active.

The half-backs again played splendidly. There is little to choose between them. Ditchfield, playing his usual game, although not a cultured artist, seems, to captivate the crowd with his clean tactics, his bull-dog tenacity, and his grand feeding of his forwards. None did- greater 'service for • his side than the captain, G. Whitfield, a veritable " Crom- well," whose influence and piloting has done much for the team.

To complete the trio; may pay tribute to " Shint " Daintith, the well-known Warrington Rugby player, whose first trial it was with the Town club? lie clearly showed ability and skill. He was never beaten, but he does stick: to the ball a little too much. However, he de- lighted the Town Committee, Who are looking forward to keeping him with them.

The Warrington forwards were not clearly in luck's way. Their finishing was not all that might be-La repetition of last week. Their shooting was bad and they would do well to practise. Combination they lack; 'individually they are artistes. ','Perhaps the Town •forwards will soon learn to "combine." Then, and then. only, can they expect to be victorious continu- ally. The outstanding men were Aspinall. Mill- ward and T. Whitfield, who 'did' much for the side and: it was Ahrough' their efforts .that :the .goals were scored. '
The team against Walkden to-day will be chosen from :—Kite, Leah, Cookson, Osborne, Ditchfield, G. Whitfield, "Shint"' •Daintith, Aspinall, Illide, Foster, Bowker, T. Whitfield, Banner and Millward.

Corporal Edwin Bowker, who is the latest recruit, for Warrington Town, and will play to-day', has served in the Gordon' Highlanders: Re has been burnt with liquid fire, gasse'd, and wounded by shrapnel. He has. however, recov- ered so far as to be able,to•resurne his football. Originally, he played for Tenaby United, while ha is a native of Bury.

A little later, however, he had another excursion along with Brookes, but again they were driven back, and Warrington took up the running.
Round the Home Goat.

Play hovered around the home goal, and finally Aspinall secured and added Warrington's second goal. From the restart the,visitors again attacked, and for quite a while penned the home team in their own quarters. Millward—who occupied the centre-forward position in the -Warrington

team—dribbled in, and had Eaves beaten all the way with a good shot. .Hayes now broke away for the Central, and, along with Brookes and Berry, worked their way into the visitors' goal- mouth, where, after a hot melee, Short scored. This stimulated Warrington to further efforts, and within a few minutes Millward broke away and added a fourth goal. Half-time arrived with the score four goals to one in favour of Warrington. _

Upon the resumption the home team attacked desperately, but good work by the visitors' backs kept them at bay. Not to be denied, Walkden came again, and this time were rewarded, for Short scored their• second goal. From now to the end give and take was the order, and shortly before time Aspinall added a fifth goal for the "Town," and the game resulted as follows :
Warrington Town, 5 goals. Walkden Central, 2 goals.

Saturday was an ideal day, and in the Junior League the sjiectators had every reason to be satisfied with the displays given for their enjoyment. •

One of the keenest games was that between the leaders of the League and the Howley United team, on the Fairfield ground, this being neutral to both teams. The Howley team was fully representative, while St. Elphin's lacked The services of Rothwell and Gleave. The game was witnessed by one of the largest crowds seen on this ground this season, and the game com- menced very keenly, and the players during the first ten minutes were too excited to do themselves justice.
The " Saints " were the first to settle down to their game, but the Howley lads proved themselves the stronger lot at all points, and ran out winners by three clear, goals:
The Howley supporters made themselves heard, both by their shouting and their rattles.
This is the fourth Saturday in succession.that the `` Saints" have been in arrears at the interval.
This is the first match in which the "Saints" have failed to score this season.
Boyle, who has proved himself to be the most consistent goal-scorer for the "Saints," was carefully watched by Bradburn, who did not allow him to take any liberties.

Walters, the Hawley custodian, by his display during the game, proved himself to be one of the best keepers in the League. He was very warmly -applauded for the way in which he saved a remarkable shot from Humphries.

Davies, Miller, Rawlinson and Walters were the most conspicuous players on the Howley team. Of the "Saints'" team, none appeared to be able to rise to the occasion, and their display was only moderate.

In the second portion the Juniors maintained their superiority and won the game by three clear goals.
By this defeat the Fairfield 'United Reserves have now lost the last chance they had of a ctaining the leadership of the League.
Instead, they have placed the St. Elphin's safely at the top of the ladder for this season.

Both teams now appeared to he tiring, and easy play followed till the call of time, when the genre was :—Howley United, 3 goals; St. Elphin's, nil.

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FE RUARY 12, 1916.

The Warrington, Runcorn and District Savings Bank tOok another step forward in ,its highly SucCessinl career on TueSday. afternoon, when a new branch office was opened at Runcorn. For years the old office has been insufficient for the increasing business of the bank, and the new establishment is an up-to-date office in Run- corn's most important thoroughfare—High- street—and for many years will serve the needs of both depositors and staff. The opening ceremony on Tuesday afternoon was performed by Mr. C. Jackson Holmes, the chairman of the Bank Management Committee. Mr. Holmes was elected to the position of chair- man at the recent annual meeting of the bank, and this was his first public function since :that event and also since the. accident he sus- tained some time ago. He has not altogether recovered from this, but on Tuesday could move about with the assistance of his friends and a cc:4le of walking stocks. Previous to the ceremony the ladies and gentlemen present assembled in front of the new bank premises for the purpose, of b6ng photographed, and included amongst those present were: Mrs. C. Jackson Holmes, Mrs. Volmar, MISS Handley, Messrs. Josiah Long- land, S. C. Beckett, John Pritchard, Thomas Wright, J. S. Hill, J. W. Hayward, Alderman J. Smethurst, Messrs. A. Stanley Wright, W.

, Banks, James Pritchard, Harris Handley, P. W. Hutton, T. D. ,Timmins, J. H. Saikeld, W. E. Lea, A. Lightburn, WM. Clegg, W. Fletcher, F. W. Hutton, James Henry Smethurst, the Rev. H. Ogden, Alderman Bennett (auditor), Messrs. Wm. ,A. Proud (chief actuary), R. Osborne (cashier), and C. Hughes (local actuary). _ _

After- the photograph had been taken, the architect, Mr. F. J. Jones, presented to Mr. Holmes a silver key withY which to open the door. Amid applause, the Chairman rose from his seats inserted the key and opened the doors, expressing the wish, that the new premises would have a long and successful career. The party adjourned to the room above the bank, where a few speeches were made, refresh- ments following.
Thrift For AU.

Mr. Holmes said it was a source of great satisfaction to him that his first public appear- ance since his accident should be to visit Run- corn to open that new office. It was hardly necessary for him to enlarge upon the subject of thrift, because the people of Runcorn seemed to know so much about it. Since the amalgama- tion with Warrington. the Runcorn deposits had increased by over JS,ooo,•but them was one thing he wished to press upon the attention or the public and that was the use of the schools
New Savings Bank Premises Opened at Runcorn.
the Runcorn Committee), and other trustees,

in saving money.. He was pleased 4o know that some of the teachers in Runcorn were endeav- ouring to instil the idea of thrift into the minds of the children. If they succeeded in doing this, they were laying a good foundation for the future.

After speaking of the early history of the Run- corn branch, Mr. S. C. Beckett referred to the endeavours of the Government to induce the workers to invest their money in the War Loan. He declared that if the Treasury had increased the interest of the Savings Banks it would have been found that the income would have been greater than it had been under the £1 war bond scheme. Though Runcorn people were fairly thrifty, there was still a certain amount of ignorance regarding the Savings Bank. Some individuals were under .the im- pression that it was ruir by a few men for their own profit, not knowing it was under the Gov- ernment.

Mr. J. Longland said he was pleased to see the new premises. He had seen a suggestion that the interest df the Post Office Savings Bank should be increased, but he failed to see why the Trustee Savings Bank should not be placed on the same footing. Tea was then served, and after the party had broken up, the bank was immediately opened for business.

It follows very closely the lines of the forecast published in "The Examiner" a fortnight ago. The area was " scheduled " on January 27th, and between then and the issuing• Of the Order deputations were received from the "Trade."

The Order applies to the whole of the two counties with certain exceptions as at Barrow- in-Furness, where an Order was already in existence, and has the full force of law without any confirmation from any other authority. While the Trade speak 3f "an affront" hav- ing been put upon the working classes and a breach of faith having been committed by the issuing of the Order before a promised inquiry had been held, the Control Board express the hope that all classes will endeavour, as far as in them lies, to secure adherence to the terms of the Order and thus Contribute in the pre- sent emergency "to the, objects which the Order is intended to promote—viz., the increase of the efficiency of labour and. the successful prosecution of the war:'

Outside these hours it is an offence to sell or supply, consume or permit to be consum d, any liquor in any licensed premises or club. -By this restriction of hours the Board hope to diminish the drinking habit, to reduce the temptations which beset munition and ti.rms- port workers, and to lessen the fa-Aqies for drinking among women, which pro ls tc deplorable extent in many localities and has in- directly a serious. effect on the efficiency Of labour.

div.head: OFF-LICENCES.
div.p: OFF-LICENCES.

The hours for off-licences are the same as above stated. f-xcept that off-licence holders must t ease serving an hour earlier in the evening than in the case of the sale for consumption on the premises.

div.head: "ORDERS" FOR SPIRITS.
div.p: "ORDERS" FOR SPIRITS.

With a desire to check the introduction of spirits into works and docks, the Board have limited the period of their sale and .dispatch for :consumption off the premises to 21 hours per day, from noon to 2.30 on the first five week- days, and have prohibited .off-Sales of spirits altogether on Saturdays and Sundays. .Further, with a view to reducing the alnises arising out of the sale of spirits in flasks and at railway stations, they have 'prohibited off- sales of spirits, in quantities legs than a reputed qua, in licensed premises and clubs, and have entirely prohibited such sales from railway refreshment-rooms.
Spirits wanted out of hours for immediate medical purposes must be ordered by means of a dated doctor's certificate. •

Spirits to be consumed off the premises must not be dispatched except on the days and dur- ing the hours specified for their sale; but it is legal to dispatch for delivery at a place more than five miles distant, in the forenoon of any day on which the sale for off-consumption is permitted.

div.p: CHECKS ON HAWKING ABUSES.

"No person shall either by himself or, by any servant or agent sell or supply any intoxicating liquor to any person in any licensed premises or in any club fox; COnstimption on the premises unless the same is ordered and paid for by the person so supplied; nor shall any person order Or pay for or lend or advance Money to pay • for any intoxicating liquor wherewith' any other person has been or is to be supplied for consump- tion on the premises; nor shall any, person con- sume in any licensed .premises or club any in- toxicating liquor which any other person has ordered or paid for or agreed to pay for or lent or advanced money to pay for." • It will be seen' that the treater, the treated, and the seller will be equally guilty of an offence here .just as all parties are responsible in'the case of a breach of the regulations as to hours 7' of opening.

This provision is based on the view, supported by scientific. and .other evidence, that the evil effects which may result from, the consumption of spirits, especially if taken without food, are likely to be less pronounced if the spirits are sold' at a reduced strength.

div.head: " MERRIE ENGLAND."
div.p: " MERRIE ENGLAND."
Music Licence Withdrawn From Socialist Hall.
PRIVILEGE ABUSED.
Merry-making in the form of whist drives and dances at the Socialist Hall, Bridge Foot, is to be no more.
Yesterday, at the Brewster Sessions, the magistrates considered that the music licence granted to them in 1911 had been abuSed and, therefore, refused to renew it.

The Chief Constable (Mr. Martin Nicholls) explained that he had received an application for renewal from Mr. Robert Rule, secretary of the British Socialist -party. The 'hall already had a music licence from 12 o'clock noon to 2.30 a.m. When the application was made in 1911, an undertaking was given by Mr. Steel, solicitor,- that the.. rooms would only be used occasionally for dances, by the friends of the members- At present, however, it had been •dis- covered that these rooms were • used on four nights per week for public whist drives and dances.

The Chief further pointed out that although the Socialist party was allowed to do this,. the licensing justices had hitherto refused a local dancing master permission to keef) open aft2r 10.30 p.m. In'the case now under consideration it was not desirable that it should be licensed to such an hour as 2.30. The functions were advertised on the door of the building, and people paid sixpence to go in. The pro- 'rioters then looked round to ti co how many people were there, and, probably finding that the takings were 30s. slipped out and got a half- crown prize. "Surely your Worships are not going to encourage this sort of thing," con- cluded •the Chief Constable.
After consulting in private. the magistrates decided not to renew the licence.
